title: Cutting Selection & Source-Plant Health
summary: A cutting begins with the physiological and health status of its source tissue. Node position, tissue maturity, hydration, pest or pathogen status, and source-plant history all influence what the propagule carries into rooting.
keyConcepts: A clone preserves the genotype of the source plant but not a guarantee of identical performance under different environments
Source plants can transmit pests and systemic pathogens without obvious symptoms
Very soft, very old, damaged, or stressed tissue can behave differently during rooting
Lot identity should connect every cutting back to its source plant
measureObserve: Record source plant ID and health status
Inspect cutting tissue and nodes before removal
Use magnification when arthropods are plausible
Keep batches separated by source and date
commonMistakes: Taking cuttings from unverified source material
Mixing cuttings from different source plants under one label
Assuming healthy appearance proves pathogen-free status
Ignoring source-plant stress history

title: Cutting Wound Response & Adventitious Rooting
summary: Rooting a cutting requires living stem tissues to survive excision, reorganize growth, and initiate adventitious roots. Wound response, carbohydrate status, hormones, oxygen, water balance, and temperature interact during this transition.
keyConcepts: A detached cutting must maintain water balance before a new root system is functional
Adventitious roots arise from responsive tissues near the stem base and vascular regions
Hormonal signals interact with tissue age and carbohydrate status
Root initiation and visible root emergence are different stages
measureObserve: Record cutting date and first visible root date
Inspect stem-base condition without repeatedly damaging tissue
Track turgor and leaf posture
Compare rooting speed among batches without assuming one cause for variation
commonMistakes: Equating callus with guaranteed root formation
Repeatedly pulling cuttings from media to check roots
Treating rooting as only a humidity problem
Ignoring stem-base decay or oxygen limitation

title: Propagation Humidity, Transpiration & Water Balance
summary: Unrooted cuttings have leaves that can lose water before roots can replace it. Propagation humidity and airflow therefore need to reduce excessive water loss without creating continuously wet, stagnant tissues.
keyConcepts: Leaf area continues to exchange heat and water after excision
High humidity can reduce atmospheric demand but does not replace stem hydration or root formation
Condensation and stagnant wetness can increase disease risk
Acclimation should increase atmospheric demand gradually as roots become functional
measureObserve: Track temperature and RH near cutting height
Inspect leaf posture and recovery
Observe condensation on leaves and enclosure surfaces
Record changes when vents or covers are opened
commonMistakes: Keeping leaves continuously wet
Opening a high-humidity enclosure abruptly
Using one room RH reading to represent the propagation microclimate
Assuming wilt always means the media is too dry

title: Rooting Media: Moisture, Oxygen & Temperature
summary: Rooting media must hold enough water to prevent desiccation while retaining pore space and oxygen. Media temperature also changes metabolic rate, water demand, and pathogen pressure.
keyConcepts: Saturation reduces air-filled pore space
Different media retain and release water differently
Warm media can accelerate metabolism while excessive heat can increase stress and disease pressure
The best moisture state depends on media properties, container geometry, and cutting demand
measureObserve: Compare media mass or moisture over time
Inspect drainage and standing water
Record media/root-zone temperature
Check whether rooting failures cluster by tray position or media batch
commonMistakes: Keeping propagation media continuously saturated
Judging internal moisture from surface color alone
Ignoring tray-edge versus tray-center differences
Changing humidity and media moisture simultaneously without records

title: Clone Sanitation & Cross-Contamination
summary: Propagation concentrates many wounds, tools, hands, surfaces, and young plants into a small area. A clean-to-dirty workflow and traceable batches reduce the chance of moving pests or pathogens through an entire clone population.
keyConcepts: Cutting tools can move biological material from plant to plant
Shared trays, domes, benches, and runoff can connect otherwise separate batches
Sanitation needs a defined method and contact process rather than an unlabeled spray bottle
Batch identity makes later investigation possible
measureObserve: Document tool-cleaning steps
Label trays by source and date
Inspect work surfaces between batches
Record any batch with unusual losses or symptoms
commonMistakes: Using one tool continuously across all source plants
Reusing dirty propagation equipment
Combining weak and healthy batches
Losing source identity after roots appear

title: Clone Acclimation & Rooted-Cutting Transition
summary: A newly rooted cutting is not automatically ready for the light, airflow, root-zone volume, and atmospheric demand of vegetative production. Acclimation should follow new root function and plant response.
keyConcepts: Root presence does not mean maximum root function
New leaves formed during acclimation can differ from leaves developed under propagation conditions
Light and VPD increases change water demand together
Transplant timing should consider root distribution and media condition
measureObserve: Inspect new-root distribution
Track leaf posture after environmental changes
Increase light or airflow in documented steps
Record recovery after transplant
commonMistakes: Moving rooted cuttings directly into much higher light
Increasing light, VPD, and irrigation strength all at once
Judging readiness only by roots visible at one hole
Allowing propagation roots to become severely root-bound before transition

title: Mother-Plant Management & Propagation Consistency
summary: Source plants used repeatedly for cuttings should be managed as tracked biological stock. Their health, age, architecture, nutrition, pest status, testing history, and cutting demand can affect propagation consistency.
keyConcepts: Mother plants are production sources, not just large vegetative plants
Repeated cutting changes canopy architecture and source-sink relationships
Systemic pathogens can spread through every cutting taken from infected stock
Source-plant replacement should preserve identity and testing history
measureObserve: Track source plant ID and age
Record cutting counts by date
Maintain health and testing records
Compare rooting outcomes by source plant
commonMistakes: Keeping source plants indefinitely without health review
Ignoring declining rooting performance by source
Mixing replacement plants without lineage records
Taking cuttings immediately after severe stress

title: Propagation Batch Metrics & Rooting Success
summary: Propagation performance is more informative when measured by batch and time rather than described as simply successful or unsuccessful. Rooting percentage, time to first roots, losses, abnormalities, and post-transplant survival describe different outcomes.
keyConcepts: Rooting percentage and rooting speed are separate metrics
Survival after transplant can reveal weaknesses not visible at first root emergence
Batch comparisons need similar starting material and environment to be interpretable
Small samples can make percentages look more precise than they are
measureObserve: Count total cuttings and rooted cuttings
Record first-root and ready-to-transplant dates
Track abnormal or lost cuttings separately
Compare post-transplant survival by batch
commonMistakes: Reporting only the best tray
Changing batch definitions midway
Ignoring post-transplant losses
Comparing different source plants as though genotype and source condition were controlled

title: Essential Elements & the Plant-Nutrition Framework
summary: Plant nutrition is the study of essential elements, their chemical forms, uptake, transport, metabolism, and interactions with the root environment. Fertilizer labels are inputs; plant nutrition is the biological system responding to them.
keyConcepts: Essentiality describes whether an element is required for a plant to complete its life cycle
Nutrient demand changes with growth rate, tissue, developmental stage, and environment
Availability in solution is not the same as successful uptake or use
Excesses can be as important as shortages
measureObserve: Know the elemental composition of major inputs when possible
Track pH and EC in context
Observe where symptoms begin and how they progress
Compare plant response with root-zone conditions and growth stage
commonMistakes: Treating every yellow leaf as one nutrient deficiency
Adding several supplements before measuring the root zone
Assuming a complete fertilizer prevents all nutrition problems
Ignoring antagonism, salinity, and water quality

title: Nitrogen Assimilation & Remobilization
summary: Nitrogen is incorporated into amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll-associated systems, and many other compounds. Its forms, uptake, assimilation, and movement within the plant matter more than leaf color alone.
keyConcepts: Plants absorb inorganic nitrogen primarily in nitrate and ammonium forms under many cultivation systems
Assimilation requires energy and carbon skeletons
Nitrogen can be remobilized from older tissues under changing supply and developmental demand
Excess nitrogen can alter growth and tissue characteristics
measureObserve: Record fertilizer nitrogen form and concentration context
Observe old-versus-new tissue patterns
Track growth rate and canopy color over time
Review root-zone EC, pH, irrigation, and environmental demand before changing nitrogen
commonMistakes: Diagnosing nitrogen status from one leaf
Assuming darker green always means better nutrition
Ignoring nitrogen form
Adding nitrogen without checking overall EC and root function

title: Phosphorus, Energy Transfer & Development
summary: Phosphorus participates in energy transfer, nucleic acids, membranes, phosphorylation, and many metabolic processes. Tissue pigmentation or slow growth alone cannot establish phosphorus limitation.
keyConcepts: Phosphate chemistry changes strongly with pH and root-zone conditions
Phosphorus participates in ATP-related energy transfer and nucleic-acid structure
Low root-zone temperature or poor root function can reduce uptake even when phosphorus is present
Excess phosphorus can interact with micronutrient availability
measureObserve: Review pH, root temperature, moisture, and root condition
Track growth rate and tissue distribution of symptoms
Use solution or tissue data where appropriate
Document phosphorus additions before increasing input
commonMistakes: Calling all purple pigmentation phosphorus deficiency
Increasing phosphorus without root-zone evidence
Ignoring cold or damaged roots
Treating bloom-stage marketing ratios as universal physiology

title: Potassium, Osmotic Regulation & Stomatal Function
summary: Potassium is a major osmotic ion involved in enzyme activation, charge balance, water relations, and guard-cell function. Its role connects nutrition directly to plant water regulation.
keyConcepts: Potassium is not built into organic molecules in the same way as nitrogen or phosphorus
Guard-cell ion movement contributes to stomatal opening and closing
Potassium demand interacts with water movement and growth
High concentrations of one cation can affect uptake of others
measureObserve: Review total root-zone EC and cation balance context
Observe leaf margins and tissue age without diagnosing from appearance alone
Track irrigation and atmospheric demand
Compare root health before changing potassium
commonMistakes: Treating marginal injury as potassium-specific
Adding potassium without checking salinity
Ignoring calcium and magnesium interactions
Separating potassium nutrition from water relations

title: Calcium Transport, Cell Walls & Signaling
summary: Calcium contributes to cell-wall and membrane function and also acts in cellular signaling. Because calcium movement is closely tied to water flow and tissue transpiration, local symptoms can involve transport as well as supply.
keyConcepts: Calcium has limited remobilization from older tissues compared with highly mobile nutrients
Young tissues depend on continuing delivery
Root health, water movement, humidity, and tissue transpiration influence distribution
Adding more calcium does not correct every calcium-like symptom
measureObserve: Inspect new growth and rapidly expanding tissues
Review irrigation continuity and root condition
Consider humidity, airflow, and leaf temperature
Review source water and fertilizer calcium before supplementation
commonMistakes: Diagnosing calcium from one necrotic spot
Ignoring root or transpiration constraints
Adding calcium into already high EC
Assuming every cultivar distributes calcium identically

title: Magnesium, Chlorophyll & Enzyme Function
summary: Magnesium sits at the center of chlorophyll and supports many enzyme systems and phosphate-related reactions. Interveinal chlorosis on older tissue can be consistent with magnesium limitation, but it is not unique to it.
keyConcepts: Magnesium is structurally central to chlorophyll
It is relatively mobile within the plant
High potassium or calcium conditions can affect magnesium uptake balance
Root-zone pH and function influence availability
measureObserve: Note whether interveinal symptoms begin on older or younger tissue
Review root-zone pH and EC
Review calcium, potassium, and magnesium input balance
Compare symptom progression after measured changes
commonMistakes: Calling all interveinal chlorosis magnesium deficiency
Adding magnesium without reviewing pH
Ignoring cation competition
Using leaf color without tissue-age context

title: Micronutrients, Cofactors & Root-Zone Chemistry
summary: Iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine, and nickel are required in smaller quantities but participate in essential enzymes, redox reactions, structure, and metabolism. Small required amounts also mean excess can become important quickly.
keyConcepts: Micronutrient availability is strongly influenced by pH and chemical form
Different micronutrients vary in mobility within the plant
Chelation can influence metal solubility and delivery
Deficiency-like symptoms can arise from root-zone chemistry even when total input is adequate
measureObserve: Record tissue age where symptoms begin
Review root-zone pH and EC
Check source-water and fertilizer micronutrient content
Avoid changing several trace elements at once when diagnosis is uncertain
commonMistakes: Treating every new-growth chlorosis as iron-specific
Stacking multiple micronutrient supplements
Ignoring pH-driven availability
Confusing total concentration with plant-available form

title: pH, Alkalinity & Root-Zone Buffering
summary: pH describes hydrogen-ion activity at a moment in time, while alkalinity describes acid-neutralizing capacity. Source-water alkalinity, media chemistry, fertilizer form, and biological activity can therefore drive root-zone pH over time.
keyConcepts: pH and alkalinity are different measurements
Water with similar pH can have very different buffering capacity
Media and irrigation frequency influence how chemistry accumulates
pH adjustment without alkalinity context can be temporary
measureObserve: Measure source-water pH and alkalinity when possible
Track root-zone pH trends rather than one isolated reading
Record fertilizer and acid/base additions
Compare input and representative root-zone measurements
commonMistakes: Using source-water pH alone to judge buffering
Chasing every small pH change
Ignoring alkalinity in repeated irrigation
Assuming runoff pH perfectly represents the whole root zone

title: EC, Salinity & Osmotic Stress
summary: Electrical conductivity estimates the ionic strength of a solution but does not identify which ions are present. High root-zone salinity can reduce the plant's ability to take up water even when the medium is physically wet.
keyConcepts: EC is a bulk conductivity measurement, not a nutrient recipe
Higher dissolved-salt concentration lowers water potential
Salinity can interact with heat and atmospheric demand
Different ion mixtures can produce similar EC values
measureObserve: Track input and representative root-zone EC
Record irrigation volume and drainage behavior
Observe wilt or tip/margin injury in context
Check source-water contribution to EC
commonMistakes: Treating EC as a direct measure of nutrient balance
Responding to high EC by adding more fertilizer
Ignoring uneven salt accumulation
Assuming wet media means water is equally available to roots

title: Genotype, Phenotype & Environment
summary: A genotype is an organism's genetic constitution; phenotype is the observed result of genotype interacting with development and environment. Breeding decisions become stronger when traits are measured across replicated environments rather than assumed to be purely genetic.
keyConcepts: The same genotype can express differently across environments
Different genotypes can respond differently to the same environment
Trait expression can change with developmental stage
Selection should distinguish repeatable genetic differences from temporary environmental effects
measureObserve: Use consistent trait definitions
Record environment with phenotype scores
Repeat observations across time or locations when possible
Keep plant identity connected to every measurement
commonMistakes: Calling every observed difference genetic
Selecting from one stressed environment without context
Changing scoring criteria during a population evaluation
Losing plant identity after harvest

title: Alleles, Homozygosity & Heterozygosity
summary: Diploid loci can carry two copies of an allele that are the same or different. Homozygosity and heterozygosity are locus-specific concepts that help explain segregation, uniformity, and the persistence of variation across generations.
keyConcepts: Homozygous and heterozygous describe allele state at a locus, not the whole plant in one word
Dominance affects phenotype but does not erase the hidden allele
Many important traits are influenced by multiple loci
Population history changes expected heterozygosity
measureObserve: Track parentage and generation
Use trait segregation as evidence rather than assuming genotype from appearance
Separate single-gene examples from polygenic traits
Use molecular data when genotype at a specific locus actually matters
commonMistakes: Calling an entire line homozygous from one visible trait
Assuming dominant means more common or better
Applying simple Mendelian ratios to every quantitative trait
Ignoring linkage and population size

title: F1, F2 Segregation & Selection
summary: Crossing genetically different parents creates an F1 population whose descendants can segregate widely in the F2. The amount and pattern of variation depend on the parents, loci involved, dominance, linkage, and population size.
keyConcepts: F1 uniformity depends on parental genetic structure
F2 populations reveal recombined allele combinations
Rare combinations require larger populations to observe reliably
Selection changes which individuals contribute to the next generation
measureObserve: Preserve parent and family identity
Score traits consistently across the full population
Record population size and selection count
Retain data on rejected as well as selected individuals when feasible
commonMistakes: Expecting every F1 from seed to be identical
Evaluating only selected plants
Calling an F2 stabilized after one generation
Ignoring population size when searching for rare combinations

title: Backcrossing & Recurrent-Parent Recovery
summary: A backcross mates a hybrid descendant back to a selected parent or related recurrent line. It can increase the contribution of the recurrent background while selection attempts to retain a target trait from the donor side.
keyConcepts: Backcrossing is a mating design, not a guarantee that every desired recurrent-parent trait returns
Selection between backcross generations matters
Linked donor DNA can remain around a target locus
Phenotype-only backcrossing can be slower or less precise for traits that are difficult to measure
measureObserve: Record recurrent and donor parent identity
Track each backcross generation clearly
Define the target trait and recurrent-background traits before selection
Use molecular markers when appropriate and available
commonMistakes: Labeling a cross BX without identifying the recurrent parent
Assuming one backcross recreates the recurrent parent
Selecting only the target trait while ignoring background performance
Losing generation records

title: Selfing, Inbreeding & Line Development
summary: Self-fertilization and other forms of inbreeding increase homozygosity over generations while exposing recessive variation and potentially concentrating both desirable and undesirable alleles.
keyConcepts: Selfing changes genotype frequencies and increases homozygosity
Greater uniformity for some traits does not mean all loci are fixed
Inbreeding can reveal recessive deleterious combinations
Selection and population management determine which lineages continue
measureObserve: Track selfed generation labels accurately
Record vigor, fertility, morphology, and target traits
Compare multiple siblings rather than only one survivor
Preserve line identity through seed storage
commonMistakes: Calling an S1 genetically identical to its parent
Assuming selfing only makes traits more stable
Ignoring inbreeding depression
Dropping records for weak or failed families

title: Population Size, Selection Intensity & Genetic Drift
summary: Small breeding populations can lose alleles by chance, while strong selection can intentionally narrow diversity. Population size and selection intensity therefore shape what variation remains available in later generations.
keyConcepts: Genetic drift is stronger in small populations
Selecting very few parents creates a bottleneck
Rare alleles can disappear even without negative selection
Maintaining multiple families can preserve options for later comparison
measureObserve: Record total population and selected parent counts
Track family representation
Document why each selected parent was retained
Preserve seed from alternate lines when diversity matters
commonMistakes: Treating ten plants as representative of a highly variable population
Selecting one standout without considering family structure
Confusing random loss with intentional selection
Discarding all unselected lineages before evaluation is complete

title: Heritability, Repeatability & Trait Selection
summary: A trait can be strongly influenced by genetics, environment, or both. Heritability is population- and environment-specific and should not be interpreted as a universal percentage describing one individual plant.
keyConcepts: Heritability describes variation within a defined population and environment
High environmental noise makes phenotypic selection less reliable
Repeated measurements can improve confidence for variable traits
Correlated traits can respond together under selection
measureObserve: Define the population and environment
Use repeatable trait measurements
Record replicate or family data when possible
Separate measurement error from biological variation
commonMistakes: Applying a published heritability value to every population
Using one subjective score for a complex trait
Ignoring environment-by-genotype interactions
Assuming a heritable trait is easy to select visually

title: Breeding Records, Pedigrees & Seed-Lot Traceability
summary: A breeding program is only as reconstructable as its records. Parent IDs, generation labels, pollination events, harvest lots, storage, phenotype data, and seed distribution should remain linked through stable identifiers.
keyConcepts: Names alone are not unique identifiers
Generation labels must reflect the actual mating event
Seed lots should connect to both parents and the pollination record
Phenotype data is more useful when linked back to seed lot and family
measureObserve: Assign stable plant and seed-lot IDs
Record parent roles and pollination date
Keep harvest and storage labels redundant
Link phenotype scorecards to plant and family IDs
commonMistakes: Renaming plants without preserving prior IDs
Mixing seed from separate pollination events
Using F/BX/S labels inconsistently
Keeping phenotype notes that cannot be traced back to a seed lot
